newsitem.title: USA: Large U.S. minority-owned firm to survive-former head.
newsitem.headline: Large U.S. minority-owned firm to survive-former head.

text.p: The nation's largest minority-owned investment banking firm, Grigsby Brandford & Co. Inc., will become much smaller but should survive in some form, its former chairman said on Thursday.

Napoleon Brandford, who left the San Francisco firm this week to join New York-based Muriel Siebert & Co. Inc., said in an interview that many of Grigsby Brandford's current employees and municipal clients would leave with him.
Brandford said the changes would weaken but should not destroy Grigsby Brandford, once considered the most powerful black-owned firm in an industry dominated by whites.
"It's a weaker firm today. Clearly, it won't be the player it had been before," he said. But he added that "the firm is still doing business" and has over $3 million in net capital.
The management shake-up at Grigsby Brandford began on Sept. 17, when Calvin Grigsby, the firm's founder and long-time chairman, abruptly announced his resignation.
After he left, it was disclosed that authorities were investigating bond deals the firm handled in Dade County, Fla. Grigsby has not been charged with any wrongdoing in the probe.
In a statement issued last week, Grigsby's attorney said his client "strongly maintains his innocence."
This week, the management shake-up at Grigsby Brandford intensified with the departures of Brandford and President Suzanne Shank, who also joined Muriel Siebert & Co.
Municipal finance experts said these significant changes would likely prove fatal to the investment banking firm, founded in 1981 by Grigsby.

The firm underwrites, sells and trades municipal bonds, preferred stock, Treasury notes and other securities. It was the only black-owned investment bank to rank in the top 15 senior managers of tax-exempt financial deals.
Brandford said he left the firm in large part because the Florida probe made it "increasingly difficult to do business."

Brandford said his new firm was likely to hire at least 30 employees away from Grigsby Brandford. Brandford said he also expected "a significant number of Grigsby Brandford's existing clients to remain loyal to those who will join the new firm."
Brandford will head up a division at the company to be called Siebert, Brandford, Shank & Co. that will handle all of the firm's municipal finance business.
"A month from now or less, Siebert, Brandford, Shank will look a lot like Grigsby Brandford's public finance effort," Brandford said.

Negotiations over the future of Grigsby Brandford were still underway, Brandford said. But people involved in the negotiations said provisions were being made to ensure that none of the firm's outstanding bond deals will suffer.
"The owners haven't decided what they're going to do yet," Brandford said. "But the firm has not and does not plan at this point to file for dissolution."
